title: Afghanistan's Sikhs
hookLine: an old Sikh community in Afghanistan shrank to a handful after attacks, and many left

lines: A HALL, A CANOPY, A KITCHEN.
cards: Sikh families once lived and traded in Afghanistan's cities, spoke the local languages, and kept their gurdwaras behind plain doorways in the old lanes of Kabul.
Step through one of those doorways: a hall with a canopy, a covered Guru Granth Sahib, a few families on the floor, a harmonium, a kitchen in the back. Then came the attacks.
A gurdwara in Kabul was struck during prayers, and worshipers were killed. After that, family after family packed what they could and left. Today is about the ones who left, and the few who stayed.

teach.b: First, the roots. Tradition says Guru Nanak's travels reached the lands to the west, and Afghan Sikhs have long told that story as part of their own.

They speak of families who lived there for generations, alongside Hindu neighbors, as shopkeepers, traders and healers who sold herbal remedies, and the gurdwara was where the community gathered. Second, the attacks.
There was more than one. A bombing in Jalalabad killed Sikh and Hindu community leaders on their way to meet the president.
Later, gunmen attacked a gurdwara in Kabul during morning prayers. A place built for gathering became the place that was hardest to gather in. Third, the leaving.

Families left for India, and from there some went on to other countries. Reports tell of saroops, copies of the Guru Granth Sahib, carried out with great care, wrapped and held high, as people do when they move the Guru.
Leaving a country is hard. Leaving it while carrying the Guru is a different kind of journey. Fourth, the text.
In a hymn of Guru Nanak, at Ang 72 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru asks how the true sangat is known, and answers: it is where the one Name is praised.

teach.h: ANG 72: WHERE THE NAME IS PRAISED.

teach.b: A few families still gathering around the Guru in a back lane are, in that line, a sangat. Size doesn't decide belonging.

how: Afghan Sikh families who settled in India, Britain, Canada and elsewhere keep their own gurdwaras and remember those killed in the attacks.

practice: Bring to mind a gathering that has grown smaller than it used to be: Afghanistan's Sikhs, if you like, or a congregation, a club, a family table with empty chairs.
Picture the few who still turn up, and with each breath out, wish them steadiness. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer or say Waheguru; if you don't, simply keep them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Afghanistan's Sikhs. An old community that, after attacks, shrank to a handful, while many families left carrying the Guru with them. Today's word.
